19. Case study: cause-specific mortality by age, sex and period

David Sarrat González

Source: vignettes/book-19-case-mortality.Rmd
book-19-case-mortality.Rmd

What you will learn

Define a calendar-year risk set, calculate cause-specific deaths and person-years, and compare crude rates by sex, age at period start and year.

You need: the Opal login from Getting started and the cause-of-death capstone. This chapter uses omop.questionnaire.

Research question

How do recorded cause-specific mortality rates differ between 2023 and 2024? The questionnaire data have deaths in both years. Everyone is observed from 2019 through 2025, with observation for this analysis stopping at death. Thus the population alive at each year’s start can contribute the whole year or time up to death. In a dataset with gaps or later entry, intersect each observation interval with the analysis year as well.

library(dsOMOPClient)
conns <- ds.omop.login("https://localhost:8443", user = "administrator",
  password = "password", resource = "omop.questionnaire", server = "site")$conns

Find the causes 

catalogue <- ds.omop.concept.lookup(c(900201L, 900202L), conns = conns)$pooled
catalogue[c("concept_id", "concept_name", "domain_id")]
concept_id concept_name domain_id
900201 Myocardial infarction Condition
900202 Pneumonia Condition 
ds.omop.concept.prevalence("death", scope = "pooled", conns = conns)$pooled
concept_id n_persons concept_name
900201 20 Myocardial infarction
900202 10 Pneumonia 
mi <- omop_event("death", 900201L)
pneumonia <- omop_event("death", 900202L)

Myocardial infarction is 900201 and Pneumonia is 900202. The inventory’s person counts are rounded down to multiples of five: 20 and 10 indicate bands 20–24 and 10–14. They are not period-specific numerators; we calculate those next.

Define age for everyone at risk

Age at death cannot classify survivors’ person-time. Use completed age at the start of the year, preserving missing age where the birth date is incomplete. Each binary cause indicator looks only within the selected year. A missing cause is distinct from no recorded death from that cause.

period_recipe <- function(start, days) {
  window <- omop_window(0, days - 1, anchor = start)
  omop_recipe(variables = list(
    sex = omop_sex(),
    age = omop_age_at(start),
    death_days = omop_time_between(start, "death"),
    mi = omop_variable(event = mi, reducer = omop_reduce("binary", window = window)),
    pneumonia = omop_variable(event = pneumonia, reducer = omop_reduce("binary", window = window))))
}
recipe_execute(period_recipe("2024-01-01", 366), out = "D_2024", conns = conns)
ds.omop.filter("D_2024", expr = omop_where(is.na(death_days) | death_days >= 0),
  newobj = "D_alive_2024", conns = conns)
ds.omop.mutate("D_alive_2024", potential_days = coalesce(death_days, 366),
  risk_days = ifelse(potential_days > 366, 366, potential_days),
  age_group = ifelse(is.na(age), "Missing", ifelse(age < 40, "under 40", "40 and over")),
  cause = ifelse(mi == 1, "Myocardial infarction",
    ifelse(pneumonia == 1, "Pneumonia", "Neither selected cause")),
  newobj = "D_risk_2024", conns = conns)

Remove people already dead before January 1. A survivor contributes 366 days in 2024; someone who dies contributes elapsed days to death, excluding the death day. We convert days to person-years using 365.25, a fixed unit conversion; it does not change the actual 366-day calendar boundary.

Look at deaths before calculating rates 

dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_risk_2024$cause",
  "D_risk_2024$sex", useNA = "always",
  datasources = conns)$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
F M NA
Myocardial infarction 4 8 0
Neither selected cause 6 6 0
Pneumonia 3 3 0
NA 0 0 0

F means female and M means male. In 2024 there are four female and eight male myocardial-infarction deaths, and three pneumonia deaths in each sex. Six people of each sex survive the year. The “Neither selected cause” row contains survivors in this dataset; in another study it could also contain other causes. The denominators include survivors’ time.

dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_risk_2024$cause",
  "D_risk_2024$age_group", useNA = "always",
  datasources = conns)$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
40 and over Missing under 40 NA
Myocardial infarction 6 6 0 0
Neither selected cause 12 0 0 0
Pneumonia 0 0 6 0
NA 0 0 0 0

Six pneumonia deaths are under 40 at period start. Six myocardial-infarction deaths are 40 or over and six have missing age. Keep the missing-age group in the calculation so that these deaths and their person-time do not disappear.

Calculate crude rates and uncertainty

The following function combines only released aggregates. Multiplying a released mean by its valid N obtains the total for that same column. Every cause indicator and the time column must describe the same complete roster. The exact Poisson interval treats person-time as fixed and deaths as a Poisson count.

released_rates <- function(table, group, year) {
  days <- dsBaseClient::ds.mean(paste0(table, "$risk_days"),
    type = "combine", datasources = conns)$Global.Mean
  py <- days[1, "EstimatedMean"] * days[1, "Nvalid"] / 365.25
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c(mi = "Myocardial infarction", pneumonia = "Pneumonia"), function(cause) {
    variable <- if (cause == "Pneumonia") "pneumonia" else "mi"
    x <- dsBaseClient::ds.mean(paste0(table, "$", variable),
      type = "combine", datasources = conns)$Global.Mean
    stopifnot(x[1, "Nvalid"] == days[1, "Nvalid"], x[1, "Nmissing"] == 0,
      days[1, "Nmissing"] == 0)
    deaths <- round(x[1, "EstimatedMean"] * x[1, "Nvalid"])
    ci <- stats::poisson.test(deaths, T = py)$conf.int * 1000
    data.frame(Year = year, Group = group, Cause = cause, People = days[1, "Nvalid"],
      Deaths = deaths, Person_years = py, Rate_per_1000 = 1000 * deaths / py,
      Lower_95 = ci[1], Upper_95 = ci[2])
  }))
}
rates_2024 <- released_rates("D_risk_2024", "All", 2024)
rates_2024
Year Group Cause People Deaths Person_years Rate_per_1000 Lower_95 Upper_95
2024 All Myocardial infarction 30 12 22.03 544.74 281.48 951.56
2024 All Pneumonia 30 6 22.03 272.37 99.96 592.84

In 2024, 30 people contribute 22.03 person-years. The myocardial-infarction rate is 544.74 per 1,000 person-years (95% CI 281.48–951.56), and the pneumonia rate is 272.37 (99.96–592.84). These intervals are wide because only 12 myocardial-infarction deaths and six pneumonia deaths support the respective rate estimates. These are crude rates: they do not adjust for the age distribution. The intentionally high mortality in this small synthetic population is a teaching example, not an estimate for a clinical population.

Use each group’s own denominator 

sex_rates <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("F", "M"), function(label) {
  ds.omop.filter("D_risk_2024", var = "sex", op = "==", value = label,
    newobj = paste0("D_sex_", label), conns = conns)
  released_rates(paste0("D_sex_", label), if (label == "F") "Female" else "Male", 2024)
}))
age_rates <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("under 40", "40 and over", "Missing"), function(label) {
  object <- paste0("D_age_", match(label, c("under 40", "40 and over", "Missing")))
  ds.omop.filter("D_risk_2024", var = "age_group", op = "==", value = label,
    newobj = object, conns = conns)
  released_rates(object, label, 2024)
}))
sex_rates
Year Group Cause People Deaths Person_years Rate_per_1000 Lower_95 Upper_95
2024 Female Myocardial infarction 13 4 9.55 418.98 114.16 1072.77
2024 Female Pneumonia 13 3 9.55 314.24 64.80 918.34
2024 Male Myocardial infarction 17 8 12.48 640.93 276.71 1262.89
2024 Male Pneumonia 17 3 12.48 240.35 49.57 702.40 
age_rates
Year Group Cause People Deaths Person_years Rate_per_1000 Lower_95 Upper_95
2024 under 40 Myocardial infarction 6 0 1.20 0.00 0.00 3076.17
2024 under 40 Pneumonia 6 6 1.20 5003.42 1836.17 10890.35
2024 40 and over Myocardial infarction 18 6 17.53 342.31 125.62 745.08
2024 40 and over Pneumonia 18 0 17.53 0.00 0.00 210.46
2024 Missing Myocardial infarction 6 6 3.30 1817.16 666.87 3955.20
2024 Missing Pneumonia 6 0 3.30 0.00 0.00 1117.22

The male myocardial-infarction rate is 640.93 per 1,000 person-years (95% CI 276.71–1,262.89), against 418.98 (114.16–1,072.77) in females. The intervals overlap. Under-40 pneumonia has six deaths in only 1.20 person-years, giving 5,003.42 per 1,000 person-years: a rate can exceed 1,000 because it is not a percentage. Age-specific rates use the age group’s own time, including survivors. A zero observed count has a positive upper confidence limit; it does not establish that the underlying rate is zero. Small cells may be withheld in other datasets; never replace a withheld result with zero.

Exercises

1. Repeat the analysis for 2023. Use 365 calendar days. Does the same number of deaths imply the same rate?

Solution 1

recipe_execute(period_recipe("2023-01-01", 365), out = "D_2023", conns = conns)
ds.omop.filter("D_2023", expr = omop_where(is.na(death_days) | death_days >= 0),
  newobj = "D_alive_2023", conns = conns)
ds.omop.mutate("D_alive_2023", potential_days = coalesce(death_days, 365),
  risk_days = ifelse(potential_days > 365, 365, potential_days),
  newobj = "D_risk_2023", conns = conns)
rates_2023 <- released_rates("D_risk_2023", "All", 2023)
rbind(rates_2023, rates_2024)
Year Group Cause People Deaths Person_years Rate_per_1000 Lower_95 Upper_95
2023 All Myocardial infarction 48 12 39.93 300.49 155.27 524.90
2023 All Pneumonia 48 6 39.93 150.25 55.14 327.02
2024 All Myocardial infarction 30 12 22.03 544.74 281.48 951.56
2024 All Pneumonia 30 6 22.03 272.37 99.96 592.84

Both years have 12 myocardial-infarction and six pneumonia deaths. The 2023 risk set contains 48 people; the 2024 risk set contains 30 after excluding 18 earlier deaths. In 2023, 39.93 person-years give rates of 300.49 for myocardial infarction (95% CI 155.27–524.90) and 150.25 for pneumonia (55.14–327.02). More person-time in 2023 gives lower rates despite equal numerators.

2. Distinguish a risk from a rate. What fraction of those alive at the start of 2024 die from each cause during that year?

Solution 2

data.frame(Cause = rates_2024$Cause,
  Deaths = rates_2024$Deaths, People_at_start = rates_2024$People,
  Percent = 100 * rates_2024$Deaths / rates_2024$People)
Cause Deaths People_at_start Percent
Myocardial infarction 12 30 40
Pneumonia 6 30 20

The risks are 40% for myocardial infarction and 20% for pneumonia over 2024. Their denominator is 30 people, whereas the rate denominator is person-years. This simple risk calculation relies on complete follow-up to death or year end.

Recap

Restrict both deaths and person-time to the same year. Define age for survivors as well as decedents, preserve missing-age time, and report counts, denominators, rates and uncertainty together.
